result:
The first time I met a man who would change my life, we were almost in a conversation that would have changed it for a different, smaller, entirely more forgettable reason. We were in the waiting area of a dentist's office in suburban Minneapolis, and I had just turned to someone to say something like "the fluorescent lights here are making me feel very young and very wrong" and he had been simultaneously turning to say the exact same thing. Our eyes met. There was a beat. A half-second where two strangers recognize the specific frequency of their own private discomfort. And then the receptionist called out both our names—two different patients, a collision of last-name initials—and the moment dissolved into a mutual, slightly embarrassed smile that was warm but not the warm I would remember decades later. The real meeting, the one that actually changed something in my life, didn't happen for another eleven months, at a conference in Chicago where I was standing in a hallway with a cold cup of coffee and he was standing with a warm one, and neither of us was trying to talk to anyone at all. We just... stopped. And the space between us became a door.

I tell this story because it sits perfectly inside the thing I want to examine: the almost. The almost-thing. The almost-conversation that becomes the true conversation. The almost-meeting that becomes the real one, but only after a long detour through ordinary life that makes the real one taste different, tastes earned.

Let me think about the word almost. It's a deceptively simple word. Almost, like almost every word, is a little machine. It does so much work in so few syllables. Almost is a bridge between is and isn't. Almost is the word that lets a statement remain true while also not being fully true. "Almost" modifies reality itself. It says: look, look, you're right there, I can see the edge of you, I'm so close that if you were just one more inch I would say yes I would say it, I would cross it, I would have it.

And there's something almost violent in that proximity. Almost is adjacent to the thing. Almost means the gap is so narrow you can feel the heat of what's on the other side. The almost-burn. The almost-fall. The almost-death. The almost-love. These compound words carry a charge, a small crack in the air, and I think this is because almost is the word we use when the thing was real enough to matter but not real enough to land.

There's a category of almost that lives in architecture. Buildings almost. A house almost, because the kitchen was supposed to be bigger, because the backyard would have been a yard and not a lawn and not a driveway, because if the lot had been the size it almost was on the property survey, the room would have been a room and not a closet. My grandmother lived in a house that was almost a house. Or not that, not quite. A house that had been almost a different house, because the blueprints in the attic showed a version of the house with a wraparound porch, a kitchen with two windows instead of one, a back door on the west side. The house she actually lived in had a small stoop, one kitchen window that faced the alley, and a back door on the south side that let in the summer heat. The almost-house exists in every house you walk into. The house you see is a decision that made another house invisible.

There's an almost that lives in cities. I drive through a city and I think, this street almost goes there, this avenue almost opens into the park, this building almost faces the river and would have a different face, different light, different life. The city is a palimpsest of almost-decisions, a stack of what-would-have-been pressed on top of what-was. The road that was built four blocks west of the one it could have been built on. The train line that was planned in 1947 and scrapped in 1973, and now there's a park there with a name no one remembers and kids slide down the old embankment on Friday afternoons. The almost-infrastructure. The ghost of the plan.

I want to talk about the almost-conversation. I have a friend, a colleague really, a person I see a few times a year, and one afternoon in October we were standing in a parking lot after some meeting that had gone badly for both of us, and I said something small and true, like "I don't know what to do with this" and he said "Neither do I," and we stood there for maybe thirty seconds, and I thought, if I say something real now, if I say the actual thing I've been carrying about him for about two years, about the way he makes me feel seen in a way I didn't know I needed, about the specific particular grief of it, then it will happen. And I opened my mouth, and my friend said something about leaving work early, and we got in our cars, and we drove away in different directions, and the almost-conversation became a small silence that I carry. Not with resentment. Not exactly. Just with the particular weight of something that was alive for a moment and then went still.

This is the thing about almosts that I find almost unbearably tender. They don't resolve. They just... exist in the body. They sit in the chest like a stone you can feel but can't quite name. You don't grieve them in the way you grieve a death, because the death is a thing and the almost is a shape of absence. You don't celebrate them, because they didn't happen. And so they just stay, unprocessed, at the edges of memory, where all the almosts gather. The almost-kiss. The almost-move. The almost-word. They form a kind of perimeter around the life you actually lived, a border.

And here's the part where I want to be honest and not romantic. Not every almost is beautiful. Some almosts are just failures dressed up in lyrical language. The almost-meeting was just a meeting. The almost-conversation was just two people getting tired. I say "almost" because I want the shape of it, the almost is part of the story. And that's fair. But I also know that sometimes I build a cathedral of meaning out of a twenty-second interaction just because the twenty seconds felt enormous at the time. The almost-music I never learned to play. The almost-language I almost spoke, the French I stopped in middle school and now only use in recipes. The almost-pianist. These almost-identities I carry around like small luggage, things I can't quite set down because they define who I am in some small way. "I almost was" a thing I say sometimes. And I mean it differently in different rooms.

The philosopher Martin Heidegger has this phrase, "Seinsvergehen," the vanishing-of-being, or what I think translates more usefully as the way existence is always already a disappearance. Every moment is an almost. The moment you're in now is already almost-gone. The thought you're having is already almost-finished. Time is a series of almosts, each one a frame in a film that's slightly too fast, and you catch the image but the image is already the next image. We move through life in this perpetual almost-present, which is why memory works the way it does. Memory is the archive of almosts. The real moment is gone, what remains is the almost, the shape of the thing, the heat-press of it.

I think about my mother's hands. Not the hands as they are now, with the age spots and the slight tremor in the left pinky, but the almost-hands. The hands that were almost-stronger, almost-smoother, almost-young. When I was small, I'd put my hand in hers at the grocery store and she'd say "you're getting too big for my grip," and it was true, but it was also almost-true, because she always held on just a little harder than necessary, and the almost was the grip, the almost-too-tight, the almost-terror. I don't think I was ever in real terror at the grocery store. I was just a small kid in a big world with bright lights and too many people. But the almost-terror was the real thing. The almost-threat in the almost-grip of the almost-caring hands.

There's an almost in the way I write. This whole essay is an almost-essay. It's almost a thing. It's almost an argument, almost a memory, almost a philosophy. It's a word that wants to be a paragraph and a paragraph that wants to be a letter and a letter that wants to be a conversation and a conversation that's almost a silence. Every form of writing is an almost-form, a thing trying to be the thing it points to. "This." The word is an almost. The finger is a gesture that is almost the thing. And language is built entirely out of this: a system of almosts that point to almosts that point to almosts, and somewhere in the chain, the actual thing that we wanted to reach is still there, just out of frame.

I'll close this by going back to the dentist's office, the almost-conversation, the almost-smile. I don't think it was the meeting that mattered. I think it was the eleven months. I think it was the time between the almost and the real, the time where I went back to work, and paid my bills, and burned garlic in a pan in an apartment where the heating was bad, and ate cold pizza at a kitchen table, and felt the world go on without the thing that I thought was important, the thing I thought the almost was pointing at. And then the conference. And the hallway. And the cold coffee and the warm coffee. And the space between us. And the door.

The almost made the real possible. The almost made the real matter. Without the almost, without the detour, without the eleven months of ordinary almost-living, the meeting in the hallway would have been just a meeting. Two people in a hallway with coffee. And maybe they would have smiled. And maybe they wouldn't have. And that's the point. That's the whole, small, unresolvable point. The almost is not a failure of the real. The almost is the real's condition. The almost is the room the real lives in. And we live in the almost so much more than we live in the real, and I don't think that's a tragedy. I think it's just where the life is. In the almost. In the gap. In the half-second where two strangers recognize the same discomfort and almost, almost, something.

And then the receptionist calls your name. And you get up. And you walk into the office. And the real thing waits, patient as a thing that knows it has all the time the world has ever given it, even though, if you think about it, it doesn't. Not really. It never will. It's already almost-gone.
